report:
**Conclusion: partly supported, but the claim is too broad.** Better *bedroom ventilation* appears to improve sleep for some people; opening a window is the intervention with the clearest experimental support. An open **door alone** lowers overnight CO₂ but has not consistently improved measured or reported sleep.

Two Danish field-intervention studies are particularly relevant. In one study of 40 bedrooms over two weeks, researchers manipulated window/door opening and measured overnight indoor air quality and sleep; the paper reports that meaningful reductions in CO₂ (at least 200 ppm) were associated with better indoor air quality and sleep-related outcomes. https://orbit.dtu.dk/en/publications/a-field-intervention-study-of-the-effects-of-window-and-door-open

In a separate field study in 29 bedrooms, opening a window, door, or both reduced overnight CO₂. But subjective and objective sleep quality and next-day performance improved **only when the window was open**—not merely when the door was opened. https://orbit.dtu.dk/en/publications/the-effects-of-bedroom-windowdoor-opening-on-bedroom-air-quality-

Earlier controlled work likewise compared a window-open condition (average CO₂ 660 ppm) with poorer ventilation (2,585 ppm), supporting a plausible ventilation/air-quality pathway, though the evidence base remains small and studies use varying sleep measures. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26452168/

**Practical takeaway:** If outdoor conditions are safe, quiet, and not polluted/allergen-heavy, opening a window or otherwise increasing fresh-air ventilation may help sleep—especially in a stuffy room. It is not a universal sleep treatment, and “open the bedroom door” is not equivalent evidence. Do not trade off fire safety: closing internal doors at night can slow smoke and fire spread. https://412firesafety.com/sleeping-with-bedroom-door-closed-fire-safety/
